claims.text: Standard melt-spinning produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbon.
The amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 structure has limited retention during reheating.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits complex crystallization behavior during reheating.
A pre-cooled, high-thermal-conductivity melt-spinning wheel can provide a more uniformly ultra-rapid quench than standard melt-spinning.
Fine-tuning wheel speed and ribbon thickness can improve the uniformity of the cooling profile.
The optimized melt-spinning setup will achieve cooling rates of 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Cooling rate significantly affects the microstructure and phase composition of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Very rapid melt-spinning suppresses crystalline phases and produces amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
A homogeneous ultra-fast quench will create a more uniform amorphous matrix with reduced local thermal gradients.
The optimized quench will reduce the number of heterogeneous nucleation sites in the amorphous matrix.
Structural inhomogeneities act as precursors or nucleation sites for crystallization during subsequent heating.
Reducing structural inhomogeneities and heterogeneous nucleation sites will limit early crystallization during reheating.
The optimized process will increase the crystallization onset temperature relative to standard melt-spinning.
The optimized process will improve retention of the glassy state during reheating relative to standard melt-spinning.
The intervention will succeed only when cooling is both sufficiently rapid and spatially uniform.
At a reduced cooling rate of approximately 52 K/s, the improved reheating stability is unlikely to occur.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy promote amorphous-phase formation in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 during extremely rapid cooling.
The exact increase in crystallization onset temperature and the degree of amorphous retention are unknown pending dedicated experiments.
